Venezuela’s Luz Andina Enters Bankruptcy, Halts Power Projects Amid Financial Crisis

CARACAS, June 10 — Luz Andina C.A., a major player in Venezuela’s electric utilities industry, has filed for bankruptcy protection following months of acute financial distress, the company announced on Monday. The insolvency has forced Luz Andina to suspend several electricity generation and transmission projects, raising questions about its future operations as the bankruptcy proceedings continue.

The Caracas-based company, which operates thermal and hydroelectric power plants across western and central Venezuela, said in a statement that it was “unable to meet its financial obligations due to persistent cash flow shortages and mounting debt.” Luz Andina indicated that it is seeking court approval for a restructuring plan but warned that ongoing uncertainty may disrupt its ability to maintain existing power supply commitments.

“Today is an extremely difficult day for our company and our employees,” Luz Andina CEO Rodrigo Gutiérrez said at a press briefing. “We are committed to working with the courts and our creditors to seek a viable path forward, but the company’s immediate priorities are stabilizing operations where possible and ensuring the safety of our workforce.”

The company’s bankruptcy filing follows steep declines in revenue and rising operating costs over the past year. According to Luz Andina, the company holds outstanding liabilities of more than $420 million, a figure that has grown rapidly since 2022. The company did not disclose the number of employees affected by the insolvency but confirmed that several planned infrastructure upgrades and plant expansions have been put on indefinite hold.

Analysts say the bankruptcy could reshape the landscape of Venezuela’s electric utilities industry, where several firms have struggled with aging infrastructure and restricted access to financing. “Luz Andina’s insolvency is a sign of the acute financial pressures facing the sector,” said Ana Isabel Paredes, an industry analyst based in Caracas. “The immediate effect is uncertainty over the company’s ability to maintain its operational footprint and deliver on existing projects.”

The National Association of Electric Utilities Employees urged management to provide clarity for workers. “We are concerned about job security and the future of ongoing projects,” the association said in a statement. “We urge Luz Andina’s leadership to engage transparently with employees and stakeholders throughout the bankruptcy process.”

The bankruptcy proceedings are ongoing, and Luz Andina said it would provide further updates as the process unfolds. Company officials declined to comment on the prospects for new investment or a possible sale of assets, citing the sensitivity of negotiations with creditors and the courts.
